taxonomyNote: NatureServe restricts A. tigrinum to the eastern tiger salamander and treats A. mavortium as a separate species; Lannoo (2005) and Animal Diversity Web use A. tigrinum in the broad sense, so the ADW range is wider than the NatureServe concept.
fieldMarks: Thick-bodied salamander 17-33 cm long with a large head and broad rounded snout.
Black background with yellow (occasionally tan or olive) blotches or spots of no fixed shape, size or position.
Belly usually yellowish or olive with invading dark pigment; about 12-13 costal grooves.
Males are proportionally longer with a more compressed tail and longer hind legs, and have a swollen vent in breeding season.
Larvae are yellow-green or olive with dark blotches, a stripe on each side and a whitish belly.
behavior: Adults live underground most of the year in self-dug burrows, found below 60 cm; surface activity is mainly during and after rain.
Migrates up to a few hundred metres between burrows and fishless breeding ponds, often on rainy nights; breeding is in spring in the north.
Eats worms, snails, insects and slugs; larvae eat aquatic invertebrates and amphibian larvae.
habitat: Found in virtually any habitat with soil suitable for burrowing and a body of water nearby for breeding; less tied to forest than other mole salamanders.
Breeds in fishless ponds, from clear mountain ponds to temporary lowland pools.
range: Eastern and central North America; Animal Diversity Web describes the broadly defined tiger salamander as ranging from southeastern Alaska to southern Labrador and south across the US to the Mexican Plateau, a range that includes forms NatureServe now assigns to other species.
